body_markdown:
Planning to tow? Not all trailers are a good fit for every type of classic car or truck. Whether it’s a fender position failure, too much tongue weight, an incompatible brake-and-hitch system, or a trailer that’s simply too bulky for the job (or too lightweight for the load), there are numerous considerations to make when trying to choose the best towing platform for your specific needs.


Designs variations ranging from single-axle dollies to open-bed dual-axle rigs, repurposed U-Haul carriers, and fully-enclosed trailers—all before we get into discussion of various different braking systems, loading ramps, tilting decks, and winch options.


The most important element, regardless of what trailer type you choose, is safety. “No matter the trailer, improper loading and securing is typically the number one failure we see,” explains Chad Anderson, Material Damage Specialist at Hagerty. “Too much weight in front of the axle or too much behind will cause a towing nightmare. A good rule to remember is the 60/40 method, with more weight in front of axle. Also consider that too short of trailer, with a loaded vehicle hanging over anywhere, is also a recipe for disaster.


“Other good things to consider are proper maintenance, well greased bearings, correct ball size, and proper tie-downs—it would not be wise to use $20 tie-downs on a $100K car, and even the best equipment won’t work if there are tears in the webbing, for instance.”


With that said, we’ve put together this guide aimed at enthusiast car owners trying to make sense of the landscape and best choices when it comes to buying, renting, or using a trailer to safely haul their vehicle.


## Open Trailers Are Easy, Breezy, and Budget-Friendly


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


An open trailer is the most common choice for most auto transport, for several reasons.


For starters, they’re the most affordable trailers out there, with entry-level models offering a simple wooden deck mounted on a steel frame and a pair of straight axles. If you’re willing to pay more, you can choose a steel or open deck (or opt for full lightweight aluminum construction) or spec fenders that drop out of the way to make it easier to open doors. Some units even tilt hydraulically or manually rather than require the use of ramps. Each of these options will appeal based on the specific needs you have for the trailer, and your budget. Prices for open trailers can range from $3,000 to upwards of $20,000, depending the materials it’s made of, the accessories and features that come with it, and its overall length.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Typically, you’ll need to do a test check to determine if the car you’re hauling has enough clearance over the fenders to get in and out without scraping the bottom sill. In these cases, a drop fender can keep you from being forced to tie down too close to the front or the rear of the trailer and potentially unbalance the load.


Those with mobility issues might also want to spring for the convenience of a tilting deck rather than have to deal with installing and stowing ramps each time they use the trailer. A tilt trailer might also be a requirement if your vehicle is extremely low, or if it has long front or rear overhangs that could make contact when transitioning from a traditional ramp to the trailer deck.


Open trailers have advantages other than pricing, of course. They can be simpler to load, especially if you have a spotter who can stand at the front or side of the deck and see the vehicle’s position at all times. Their lack of visual bulk generally offers better sightlines when reversing, which can make them easier to maneuver in tight spaces.


[Benjamin Hunting](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bhunting/)


They also offer full access to the vehicle once it’s loaded, letting you pop the hood, hatch, or trunk, and open the doors with ease, as well as quickly adjust tie-down straps that might have loosened during transport. Finally, you can keep an eye on your car at all times, making it easy to spot if it’s shifted position or if a strap has come loose.


Unsplash/Calvin Kertzman


That being said, open-deck trailers come with one glaring weakness: absolutely zero protection for your vehicle. Sure, you can find designs that include a shield at the front of the deck intended to clock both wind and debris, but it can only do so much. The reality is an open trailer leaves your vehicle exposed to the elements, to rocks and other junk kicked up from the road, and to the prying eyes of would-be thieves. Even if you don’t end up with a bunch of rock chips, you’ll still be cleaning your vehicle once you reach your destination.


## The Open Trailer With the Greatest Risk: Tow Dolly


Flickr/oddharmonic


There’s one specific type of open trailer that bears special mention, and that’s the transport dolly. By far the cheapest way to tow a vehicle from A to B, these single-axle contrivances are intended to slip under one set of wheels and tug your car along while it rides on the other.


Unless you have no other options, or are moving a parts vehicle, a tow dolly should be avoided. They can put significant stress on your vehicle (which was never designed to roll long distances at this kind of angle), offer minimal points of attachment, and could in theory damage your transmission or running gear if the car is not properly prepared (such as by the removal of the driveshaft). They are not a particularly secure method for moving a classic you care about, either.


Flickr/James Tworow


## Enclosed Trailers Offer Protection, At A Price


Robert Cianflone/Getty Images


Enclosed trailers in many ways create a rolling garage for your vehicle, serving as a shield against weather and abuse. Closed designs are perfect for those seeking to protect a high-dollar restoration, vehicles that don’t have a roof or side glass, or ones that the owner/shipper would rather keep under the radar.


Closed trailers also mean secured space for hauling additional items (along with the car in question) that an open design would have more difficulty accommodating. Simply put: it’s easier to throw tools, tires, coolers, chairs, and covers inside a closed trailer without worrying about them flying around mid-trip or being stolen once your rig is parked. It also keeps them safe from the same rain, snow, and road debris that would otherwise threaten a vehicle.


Unsplash/John Cameron


Remember what we said about garages on wheels? That’s another plus that comes with any enclosed trailer: the ability to use it as a storage spot at home if you run out of bays in your actual garage. Depending on how much cash you want to splash out, you can even add a generator and air conditioner to an enclosed setup to keep things cool and comfortable trackside or at a concours event, making them feel like a mobile home away from home.


Speaking of cash: Enclosed trailers generally cost more than comparably-sized open trailers, due to the additional materials and labor required to construct them. The sky can be the limit here: expect a floor of around $8,000 for a very basic enclosed trailer, with over-$40,000 price tags for double-decker setups or towable Garage-Mahals. Then there’s the weight penalty of the roof and walls, and the structure that support them. Combine that with the generally terrible aerodynamics of a basic squared-off design, and you’re also looking at reduced performance from your tow vehicle in terms of passing power and fuel economy.


Flickr/Trailers of the East Coast


The bulk of an enclosed trailer can make them difficult to park, store, and generally deal with, as sightlines are blocked by its walls. For larger units, you might have to spring for a camera system to be able to reverse with confidence, and since they lack the low profile of an open trailer, you’ll be staring at it while it’s sitting around the yard. (Some newer trucks come equipped with useful trailer cameras.)


There are a few other pain points to keep in mind when considering an enclosed trailer. You’ll need to make sure that your vehicle actually fits inside before committing. Do a reality check with a tape measure to ensure that mirrors, antennas, roll bars, and bumpers don’t protrude past where the trailer can accommodate.


Unsplash/Drake


It can be more difficult to load a vehicle into an enclosed trailer (especially if the angle of the ramp door at the rear is too abrupt), not to mention finding one that offers you an escape door that’s properly positioned so you can exit the car after you’ve driven it inside the carrier. You don’t want to be squeezing out through a tiny opening between the wall and your car’s paint, or crawling through a window because you can’t open the door.


Finally, theft remains an issue, even for enclosed trailers. Thieves are often opportunists, but some bad actors might assume that since you’ve taken extra steps to protect your vehicle, it’s potentially valuable enough for them to take a risk with a break-in. This is especially true if you’re storing your classic in the trailer on your property, where it could make for a more tempting target. Since you can keep a lot of stuff inside your trailer alongside your car, if your rig does get stolen, you could end up losing more than just your ride.


## Size Matters and So Does Weight


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Over and above the open-versus-enclosed debate, choosing the right trailer size is key to a smooth towing experience. You want a design that balances the position of your car so that you have plenty of space to tie it down, while also giving your wiggle room front and rear to put the correct tongue weight on your hitch. At the same time, you don’t want a trailer that is too long, as it will be more of a hassle to deal with while underway, and potentially cause sway and balance issues with your tow rig. The smallest trailer that accommodates your vehicle will be the easiest to deal with, the lightest to tow, and the cheapest to maintain over time.


Flickr/Trailers of the East Coast


You will also need to ensure that a trailer’s gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) and payload capacity match up with your needs. The GVWR represents the total weight that the trailer can handle, including its own weight, while the payload represents the GVWR minus the trailer’s own weight.


It’s important to not get these two numbers confused. A trailer with a GVWR of 7000 pounds can’t haul a 7000 pound car, for example. If that trailer weighs 3000 pounds empty, that leaves you with just 4,000 pounds left over before you reach the unit’s limits. Also keep in mind how much overhead you’ll need to accommodate spares, tires, and tools that you plan to bring those along. You’ll have to add that on top of the weight of the car to determine whether the trailer in question can handle the entire load. Naturally, you also need a tow vehicle that can safely handle the total load.


## Accessories That Can Make Or Break


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Trailers are a bit like Lego in the sense that you can add or remove various accessories to make your life easier, save some weight, or streamline maintenance.


Popular add-ons for all trailer types are overhead tire racks, along with winches (both mechanical and electrical) to help load stalled or otherwise disabled autos. Open trailers can be made more practical with external lockable storage bins that typically ride like saddle bags at the rear. Tilt decks are something that need to be specified at ordering time, as there’s no practical way to convert an existing trailer to this kind of design, but you can always attach a set of ramp extenders to assist with loading on any trailer type.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


You’ll also need to decide what type of braking system makes the most sense for your tow rig. The vast majority of car haulers use electric braking systems that connect to your tow rig via the trailer’s wiring harness. These are versatile, and easy to maintain systems that are generally trouble-free, offering adjustability via a trailer brake controller from inside the vehicle.


There are a subset of car haulers out there, however, that use a different technology called surge braking. These are self-contained designs that transform energy from the trailer that momentum applies to the hitch when slowing down, converting it into hydraulic pressure that activates the trailer’s brakes. There is no wiring required.


Kypros/Getty Images


Surge brakes are uncommon for car haulers, as they are mostly used on boat trailers and utility trailers. That being said, every U-Haul car trailer uses a surge braking system, and since many of these rental units eventually end up in private hands, you’ll need to verify the system that’s installed on the trailer you’re considering buying. The situation gets more complicated if you’re considering using a weight-distributing hitch. This popular towing add-on helps reduce trailer sway and improve stability, but because it arrests the motion of the trailer neck, most weight-distributing hitches are not compatible with a surge brake setup and can lead to a dangerous situation out on the road if used.


## Know What You’re Towing, Save Some Cash


[Matthew Anderson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/manderson/)


It’s easy to be overwhelmed by all of the above choices. The single best piece of advice when it comes to choosing a trailer is to have a good understanding of the type of towing you’ll be doing the most often. Avoiding the temptation to buy more trailer than you need—whether it’s length or weight capacity—will save you serious cash. If your tow vehicle has enough muscle, you can also probably skip springing for a lightweight aluminum chassis.


In addition, be realistic about how much protection from the elements you need while towing. If your car is usually stored outside, or isn’t a concours-level restoration, you can probably do without an enclosed hauler. Finally, pay only for the accessories that will save you time and hassle (tilt, winch), rather than the ones you might only ever need to use occasionally.
